t: CPR: when someone is not breathing
k: cpr resuscitation cardiac arrest heart not breathing unconscious compressions cpr: when someone is not breathing chest compressions save lives
b: p
If a person does not respond and is not breathing normally, their heart has probably stopped. Every minute without CPR lowers the chance of survival.
ol
Check the area is safe for you.
Shout and tap the shoulders. No answer and no normal breathing (gasping does not count)? Start now.
Call 112 on speaker, or send someone. Ask for a defibrillator (AED) if there is one nearby.
Kneel beside the chest. Heel of one hand in the centre of the chest, other hand on top.
Push hard and fast: 5-6 cm deep, 100-120 times a minute. Let the chest rise fully between pushes.
If trained and willing: after 30 compressions give 2 rescue breaths. If not, do compressions only without stopping.
Do not stop until help arrives, the person wakes up and breathes normally, or you are physically exhausted.
w
Compressions only are much better than doing nothing. In a remote place, keep going and swap with others every 2 minutes.

k: recovery position unconscious breathing side vomit airway recovery position unconscious but breathing
b: p
An unconscious person lying on their back can choke on their tongue or vomit. If they breathe normally, turn them on their side.
ol
Kneel beside them. Put the arm nearest you at a right angle, palm up.
Bring the far arm across the chest and hold the back of that hand against their near cheek.
Bend the far knee up, foot flat on the ground.
Pull on the far knee to roll them towards you onto their side.
Tilt the head back slightly so the airway stays open and the mouth points down.
Keep them warm, call 112 and check breathing every minute.
w
If you suspect a spine injury (fall from height, high speed), move them only if they vomit or you must leave them, and keep head and body in line.

k: choking choke food stuck throat heimlich airway cough choking back blows and abdominal thrusts
b: p
If the person can cough, speak or breathe, encourage them to keep coughing. Act only if they cannot breathe, speak or cough.
ol
Stand beside and slightly behind them, support the chest and lean them forward.
Give up to 5 sharp blows between the shoulder blades with the heel of your hand.
If that fails, stand behind them, fist just above the belly button, other hand over it, and pull sharply inwards and upwards up to 5 times.
Alternate 5 back blows and 5 thrusts.
If they become unconscious, call 112 and start CPR.
w
After abdominal thrusts the person must be checked by a doctor, even if they feel fine.

s: Press hard and do not let go
k: bleeding blood wound cut hemorrhage pressure bandage severe bleeding press hard and do not let go
b: p
Heavy bleeding can kill in minutes. Your hands are the first tool.
ol
Protect yourself with gloves or a plastic bag if you can.
Press firmly on the wound with a clean cloth, bandage or your hand.
Keep pressing for at least 10 minutes without lifting to look.
If blood soaks through, add more cloth on top and keep pressing.
Wrap tightly with a bandage to keep the pressure.
Lay the person down, keep them warm and call 112.
w
For bleeding from an arm or leg that does not stop with pressure, a tourniquet can save a life. See the tourniquet guide.

k: tourniquet bleeding arm leg amputation belt windlass tourniquet last resort for limb bleeding
b: p
Use a tourniquet only for life-threatening bleeding from an arm or leg that strong direct pressure cannot stop.
ol
Place it 5-8 cm above the wound, never on a joint.
A commercial tourniquet is best. Improvised: a band at least 4 cm wide (scarf, triangular bandage), tied around the limb with a stick to twist it.
Twist until the bleeding stops. It will hurt: that is normal.
Secure the stick so it cannot unwind.
Write the time it was applied on the skin or on tape.
Do not loosen it. Call 112 and say a tourniquet is on.
w
Never use thin cord, wire or a narrow strap: they cut the skin and do not stop the bleeding.

k: wound cut scrape graze clean infection disinfect dressing cleaning small wounds stop infection before it starts
b: ul
Wash your hands first.
Rinse the wound with plenty of drinking water: pressure helps wash out dirt.
Remove small debris with clean tweezers.
Cover with a clean dressing and change it daily.
Signs of infection: growing redness, heat, swelling, pus, red streaks, fever.
w
See a doctor for deep wounds, animal bites, wounds that gape open, or if you are not vaccinated against tetanus.

s: Stop them before they stop you
k: blister feet foot hot spot boots socks blisters stop them before they stop you
b: p
A blister starts as a hot spot. Stop as soon as you feel rubbing.
ul
Hot spot: dry the skin, cover with tape or a blister plaster.
Small intact blister: leave the skin on and protect it with a donut of padding.
Large painful blister: clean, pierce at the edge with a sterilised needle, press the fluid out, keep the roof skin and cover.
Change wet socks, keep laces even, cut toenails before the trip.
w
Watch for infection: redness spreading or pus.

k: sprain ankle twisted knee ligament swelling sprained ankle can you still walk out?
b: ul
Stop, sit and check: can you bear weight for 4 steps? If not, it may be broken.
Cool it with cold water or snow wrapped in cloth, 15 minutes at a time.
Wrap with an elastic bandage in a figure of eight, not too tight.
Raise the leg when resting.
Walking poles take weight off; keep the boot on and laced firmly to support it.
w
Strong pain on the bone, deformity, or numb toes: treat as a fracture and call for help.

k: fracture broken bone splint arm leg immobilize fractures and splints keep it still
b: ol
Do not try to straighten a deformed limb.
Support it in the position you found it.
Splint it: pad with clothing and fix it to something rigid (poles, sticks, a rolled sleeping mat) including the joints above and below.
Check fingers or toes: they should stay warm and pink.
Arm: a sling with a scarf or jacket. Leg: tie it to the other leg with padding between.
Keep the person warm and call 112.
w
Open fracture (bone through the skin): cover with a clean dressing, do not push the bone back.

k: head injury concussion fall knock unconscious helmet head injury when a bump becomes dangerous
b: p
After a blow to the head, watch the person closely for 24 hours.
ul
Call 112 if they were knocked out, even briefly.
Danger signs: worsening headache, repeated vomiting, confusion, drowsiness, unequal pupils, fluid from the nose or ears, seizure, weakness of one side.
Do not let them continue a difficult route.
Keep them company and do not let them sleep alone that night.
w
With a fall from height, also suspect a neck injury: keep head and neck still.

s: When the body gets too cold
k: hypothermia cold shivering wet wind confusion hypothermia when the body gets too cold
b: p
Hypothermia can happen at 10 °C with wind and rain, not only in snow.
ul
Early signs: strong shivering, clumsy hands, bad mood, slow thinking.
Severe signs: shivering stops, confusion, drowsiness. This is an emergency.
Get out of wind and wet, into shelter.
Replace wet clothing with dry layers, add a hat and insulation under them.
Warm sweet drinks if they can swallow safely.
Warm the chest, armpits and neck with warm (not hot) bottles or body heat.
w
Handle a severely hypothermic person very gently: rough movement can trigger heart rhythm problems. Call 112.

s: Freezing of fingers, toes, nose and ears
k: frostbite frozen fingers toes cold numb white frostbite freezing of fingers, toes, nose and ears
b: ul
Early stage (frostnip): skin white and numb, soft. Warm it with body heat: hands in armpits, feet on a partner's belly.
Deep frostbite: skin hard, waxy, grey-white.
Do not rub with snow or massage.
Rewarm only if it will not freeze again: refreezing does much more damage.
Rewarm in water at 37-39 °C (comfortable for an elbow) for 30 minutes.
Do not burst blisters. Cover loosely, keep dry.
w
If you must walk out on frozen feet, it may be better to walk before rewarming. Get medical help.

k: heat heatstroke exhaustion sun hot sweating dizzy heat exhaustion and heatstroke too hot can kill
b: ul
Heat exhaustion: heavy sweating, weakness, headache, nausea, dizziness. Rest in shade, drink water with salts, cool the skin.
Heatstroke: hot skin, confusion, strange behaviour, collapse. This is an emergency: call 112.
Cool fast: wet the whole body, fan it, cold packs at neck, armpits and groin.
Prevention: start early, rest in shade, drink regularly, wear a hat.
w
Do not give drinks to someone who is confused or drowsy: they may choke.

k: sunburn snow blindness uv eyes sunglasses altitude sunburn and snow blindness light is stronger up high
b: ul
UV increases about 10% every 1,000 m of altitude, and snow reflects up to 80%.
Use sunscreen SPF 30-50 and reapply every 2 hours.
Wear category 3-4 sunglasses on snow and glaciers, also when cloudy.
Snow blindness: burning, gritty eyes hours later. Rest in the dark, cool compresses, no rubbing. It heals in 1-2 days.
No sunglasses? Cut thin slits in cardboard or fabric to cover the eyes.

k: altitude sickness mountain ams headache high hace hape acclimatize altitude sickness climb high, sleep low
b: p
Above about 2,500 m many people get acute mountain sickness.
ul
Symptoms: headache plus nausea, tiredness, dizziness, poor sleep.
Above 3,000 m, raise your sleeping altitude by no more than 300-500 m per day.
Mild symptoms: stop climbing and rest until they go.
Worsening symptoms: go down at least 300-500 m.
Danger signs: confusion, loss of balance, breathlessness at rest, gurgling cough. Go down immediately and call for help.
w
Never climb higher with symptoms of altitude sickness.

k: lightning struck strike thunderstorm burns cpr struck by lightning help them right away
b: p
A person struck by lightning does not carry an electrical charge: you can touch them safely.
ul
Move to a safer place if the storm continues.
If they are not breathing: start CPR immediately. Lightning victims often recover with fast CPR.
Multiple victims: first help those who appear dead.
Check for burns, fractures and hearing loss. Call 112.

k: burn burns fire scald hot water stove burns cool water, 20 minutes
b: ol
Stop the burning: smother flames, remove hot clothing unless stuck.
Cool the burn under cool running or clean water for 20 minutes.
Remove rings and watches before swelling.
Cover loosely with cling film or a clean plastic bag.
Keep the rest of the body warm.
w
Call 112 for burns larger than the person's hand, on the face, hands, feet or genitals, or if smoke was inhaled. No butter, oil or toothpaste.

k: sting bee wasp hornet allergy anaphylaxis epipen swelling stings and allergic reactions know anaphylaxis
b: ul
Bee sting: scrape the stinger out sideways with a fingernail or card.
Cool the area. Antihistamine helps itching.
Stings in the mouth or throat: suck ice and call 112.
Anaphylaxis: swelling of face or tongue, difficulty breathing, hives, collapse. Call 112.
If they have an adrenaline auto-injector, help them use it in the outer thigh, through clothing.
Lay them down with legs raised, or sitting if breathing is hard.

s: Steady pull, the sooner the better
k: tick removal lyme tbe encephalitis bite removing a tick steady pull, the sooner the better
b: ol
Use fine tweezers or a tick hook as close to the skin as possible.
Pull straight out slowly and steadily, or twist with a tick hook.
Do not squeeze the body, burn it or cover it with oil.
Disinfect the spot and note the date.
Watch for 30 days: an expanding red ring, fever or flu-like illness need a doctor.
w
In many Alpine areas ticks carry TBE (tick-borne encephalitis): ask your doctor about vaccination.

k: bite dog animal fox bat rabies wound animal bites wash, cover, see a doctor
b: ul
Wash the bite with soap and running water for 15 minutes.
Cover with a clean dressing.
See a doctor: animal bites easily get infected and may need antibiotics, tetanus or rabies vaccination.
Bats, foxes and wild animals that behave strangely: always ask about rabies, even for a scratch.

k: dehydration thirst water urine salts electrolytes dehydration drink before you are thirsty
b: ul
Signs: thirst, dark urine, headache, tiredness, dizziness when standing.
On the trail drink about 0.5 l per hour, more in heat.
Add salts on long hot days: a pinch of salt and sugar in water works.
Pale yellow urine means you drink enough.
w
Drinking huge amounts of plain water for hours without salt can also be dangerous.

k: diarrhea diarrhoea stomach vomiting food water illness diarrhoea on the trail replace water and salt
b: ul
Drink small sips often: oral rehydration salts, or 1 l clean water with 6 teaspoons sugar and half a teaspoon salt.
Eat plain food when you can.
Wash hands with soap or gel before eating and after the toilet.
See a doctor for blood in the stool, high fever, or if it lasts more than 3 days.

k: eye dust grit foreign body rinse something in the eye rinse, do not rub
b: ul
Do not rub.
Rinse with plenty of clean water from the inner corner outward.
Pull the upper lid over the lower one to sweep out grit.
Anything stuck in the eye or chemicals: cover both eyes loosely and get help.

k: nosebleed nose bleeding nosebleed lean forward, pinch
b: ul
Sit and lean forward, not back.
Pinch the soft part of the nose for 10-15 minutes without letting go.
Breathe through the mouth, spit out blood.
If it lasts more than 30 minutes or follows a blow to the head, get help.

k: hypoglycemia diabetes sugar low shaking sweating low blood sugar fast sugar, then food
b: ul
Signs: shaking, sweating, pale skin, hunger, confusion, strange behaviour.
If they can swallow: give fast sugar (sweet drink, glucose tablets, sugar cubes).
After 10-15 minutes, if better, give slower food like bread or a bar.
If they are drowsy or cannot swallow: nothing by mouth, recovery position, call 112.

k: asthma breathing inhaler wheeze asthma attack sit up, use the inhaler
b: ul
Help them sit up, leaning slightly forward. Stay calm.
Help them use their reliever inhaler (usually blue): 1 puff every 30-60 seconds, up to 10 puffs.
Call 112 if there is no improvement, they cannot speak in sentences or lips turn blue.
Cold air and effort trigger attacks: a scarf over the mouth helps.

s: The surest way to kill germs
k: boil boiling water purify altitude germs boiling water safely the surest way to kill germs
b: ul
Bring water to a rolling boil for 1 minute; above 2,000 m boil for 3 minutes.
Filter cloudy water through a cloth first.
Boiling kills bacteria, viruses and parasites, but does not remove chemicals or salt.
Let it cool covered so it stays clean.

k: tablets chlorine dioxide iodine purify water purification tablets and drops light, cheap, slow
b: ul
Chlorine dioxide tablets work against bacteria, viruses and most parasites.
Read the waiting time: usually 30 minutes, up to 4 hours in very cold or dirty water.
Filter or let cloudy water settle first: dirt protects germs.
Iodine is not for pregnant people or those with thyroid problems.

k: filter water squeeze pump straw virus bacteria water filters which one does what
b: ul
Hollow-fibre filters (0.1-0.2 micron) stop bacteria and parasites, not viruses.
In Europe's mountains viruses in water are rare upstream of houses; near villages or livestock, add tablets or boil.
Never let a used hollow-fibre filter freeze: it can crack without you noticing. Sleep with it in your sleeping bag in cold weather.
Backflush after each trip.

s: A clear bottle and 6 hours of sun
k: sodis sun uv bottle water disinfection sun disinfection (sodis) a clear bottle and 6 hours of sun
b: ul
Fill a clear PET plastic bottle (up to 2 l) with clear water.
Lay it flat in full sun for 6 hours, or 2 days if cloudy.
Works only with clear water: if you cannot read a newspaper through the bottle, filter it first.
Emergency method: better than drinking untreated water.

s: Melt it, do not eat it
k: snow melt water winter stove dehydration water from snow melt it, do not eat it
b: ul
Eating snow cools your body and wastes energy: melt it instead.
Put a little water in the pot first, then add snow, so the pot does not scorch.
Snow melts to about a tenth of its volume: it takes a lot of fuel.
Old granular snow and ice give more water than fresh powder.
Snow can be dirty: treat it like any other water near huts and paths.

k: find water spring stream valley green vegetation finding water read the landscape
b: ul
Water flows downhill: look in valleys, gullies and at the foot of cliffs.
Bright green plants, reeds, willows and alders show water nearby.
Birds flying low and straight at dawn and dusk often head to water.
Map symbols: blue lines, springs, troughs and huts.
Collect rain with a jacket or tarp; collect dew with a cloth at dawn.
w
Avoid water below pastures, mines, roads and towns.

k: fire triangle heat fuel oxygen burn how fire works heat, fuel and air
b: p
Fire needs three things: heat, fuel and air. Take one away and it dies; that is also how you put it out.
ul
Build from small to big: tinder, kindling the thickness of a pencil, then thumb-thick sticks, then wrist-thick fuel.
Prepare everything before you light: a fire fails in the first minute.
Leave gaps for air, and blow gently at the base.

k: tinder birch bark grass fungus resin fatwood cotton natural tinder what catches a spark
b: ul
Birch bark: burns even when damp, thanks to its oils.
Dry grass, thistle down, cattail fluff.
Resin-rich pine wood (fatwood) shavings.
Inner bark of dead cedar or juniper, rubbed into fluff.
Carry your own: cotton balls with vaseline burn for minutes.

s: Dry wood from inside wet wood
k: feather stick knife carving wet wood kindling feather sticks dry wood from inside wet wood
b: ol
Split a dead branch to reach the dry wood inside.
Hold the knife at a low angle and push long thin curls down the stick without cutting them off.
Make a bunch of curls at the bottom of each stick.
Light the thinnest curls; make 3 or 4 sticks.

k: ferro rod ferrocerium flint striker spark firesteel ferro rod sparks in any weather
b: ul
Hold the rod on the tinder and pull the rod back while the striker stays still: you will not scatter the tinder.
Scrape firmly with the back of a knife or the striker.
Sparks reach about 3,000 °C: they need very fine dry tinder.
Works wet and at altitude, unlike matches and lighters in the cold.

k: teepee log cabin star fire lay cooking fire lays teepee, log cabin and star
b: ul
Teepee: sticks leaned over the tinder. Fast to start, good for heat and light.
Log cabin: square layers around a small teepee. Stable, makes coals for cooking.
Star: long logs pushed into the centre as they burn. Saves wood through the night.
Long log (reflector): a wall of logs or rocks behind the fire throws heat towards you.

k: fire rain wet damp kindling shelter fire in the rain dry inside, shelter above
b: ul
Find dead branches still on trees, not on the ground.
Split wood to reach the dry core; make feather sticks.
Build on a platform of sticks, not on wet soil.
Shield the fire with your body, a tarp or a rock while it starts.
Keep spare tinder in your pocket, dry with body heat.

k: extinguish fire out ashes water forest fire leave no trace putting a fire out cold to the touch
b: ol
Let the wood burn down to ash.
Pour water slowly and stir the ashes, then pour again.
Feel with the back of your hand: it must be cold.
Scatter cold ashes and leave no trace.
w
Many regions ban open fires in summer or in forests. A fire can creep underground through roots and peat for days.

s: Never cook in a closed tent
k: stove gas carbon monoxide tent cooking poisoning stoves and carbon monoxide never cook in a closed tent
b: ul
Cook outside or in a very well ventilated porch.
Carbon monoxide has no smell: headache, dizziness and drowsiness are warning signs.
Gas canisters work poorly below 0 °C: keep them warm in your jacket.
Check fittings and keep the stove stable on flat ground.

k: camp spot tent site choose wind water rockfall choosing a camp spot where to sleep safely
b: ul
Flat, slightly raised ground: cold air and water collect in hollows.
Away from dead trees and branches that can fall.
Not in dry riverbeds or close to streams that can flood in a storm.
Not under cliffs or on avalanche and rockfall paths.
Shelter from the wind behind boulders or trees, door away from the wind.
At least 60 m from lakes and streams.

k: tent wind pitch storm guy lines pegs pitching a tent in wind narrow end into the wind
b: ul
Pitch the narrow, low end into the wind.
Peg the windward side first, while the tent is still flat.
Use all guy lines; in soft ground use rocks on top of pegs or bury sticks as anchors.
Keep the tent in your hand or tied at all times: a gust can take it away.

k: bivouac emergency night shelter cold survival blanket emergency night out survive until morning
b: ul
Decide early, while there is light, to stop and prepare.
Get out of the wind: behind rocks, in a hollow, among trees.
Insulate from the ground with your pack, rope, branches or leaves: the ground steals more heat than the air.
Put on every layer, hat and gloves; feet in the pack.
A survival blanket or bag around you, and stay close to others.
Eat something before sleeping: digestion makes heat.

k: tarp shelter a-frame lean-to ridge line tarp shelters light roof, many shapes
b: ul
A-frame: a ridge line between two trees and the tarp over it, both sides pegged. Good in rain.
Lean-to: one edge high, one pegged low into the wind. Good with a fire in front.
In wind and rain, keep the tarp low and steep.
Tie a drip line on the ridge so water does not run along it into the shelter.

k: sleeping bag cold night warm mat insulation sleeping warm small tricks, big difference
b: ul
Your mat matters as much as the sleeping bag: look at its R-value (4 or more in winter).
Eat and drink something warm before bed.
Change into dry clothes and wear a hat.
A bottle of hot water in a sock at your feet or between your thighs.
Do a few minutes of exercise to warm up before getting in, without sweating.
Pee before sleeping: your body wastes heat keeping it warm.

k: bivouac hut bothy shelter refuge mountain etiquette bivouacs and huts unstaffed shelters in the mountains
b: ul
Unstaffed bivouacs are for everyone and especially for emergencies: never reserve them.
Leave them cleaner than you found them; take all rubbish down.
Leave dry wood for the next person if there is a stove.
Write in the hut book: it can help rescuers.
Close doors and windows properly: snow and animals get in.

s: See mountains on a flat map
k: contour lines topo map relief slope steep valley ridge reading contour lines see mountains on a flat map
b: ul
Each contour line joins points at the same height.
Lines close together mean steep ground; far apart means gentle.
Contours pointing like a V uphill show a valley or gully; V pointing downhill show a ridge or spur.
Closed circles are summits or hollows.
Learn the contour interval of your map (often 10 or 25 m).

s: From the map to the ground
k: compass bearing map direction azimuth taking a bearing from the map to the ground
b: ol
Put the compass edge on the map from where you are to where you want to go.
Turn the dial until its lines match the map's north-south grid lines, N to the north.
Take the compass off the map, hold it flat in front of you.
Turn your whole body until the red needle sits inside the red arrow on the dial.
Walk where the direction arrow points; pick a landmark on that line and walk to it.
w
Keep the compass away from phones, metal and magnets. In the Alps magnetic declination is small (a few degrees east).

t: Where am I on the map?
k: triangulation resection position locate lost map compass where am i on the map? two bearings, one position
b: ol
Find two landmarks you can see and identify on the map, ideally at 60-120° from each other.
Take a bearing to each one.
On the map, draw a line from each landmark along the back bearing.
You are where the lines cross. A third landmark makes a small triangle: you are inside it.

k: sun direction south shadow stick watch navigation direction from the sun no compass needed
b: ul
In the northern hemisphere the sun is roughly south at midday (about 13:00 in summer time).
Shadow stick: mark the tip of a stick's shadow, wait 15 minutes, mark again. The line from the first to the second mark points roughly east.
The sun rises in the east and sets in the west, but only exactly on the equinoxes.

k: stars polaris north star big dipper night navigation direction from the stars find north at night
b: ul
Find the Big Dipper (Great Bear).
Follow the two stars at the end of its pan about five times their distance: you reach Polaris, the North Star.
Polaris is almost exactly above north; its height above the horizon is about your latitude.
Southern hemisphere: use the Southern Cross.

k: moss north myth tree rings ants navigation navigation myths moss is not a compass
b: ul
Moss grows where it is damp and shady, not reliably on the north side.
Tree rings and anthills are not reliable either.
Wind-shaped trees can help, but only if you know the local prevailing wind.
Reliable: sun, stars, map, compass, GPS, and following water downhill to valleys and paths.

k: lost stop think observe plan disoriented if you are lost: stop stop, think, observe, plan
b: ul
Stop: sit down, drink, eat something. Panic makes things worse.
Think: where was the last place you were sure of your position?
Observe: map, GPS, landmarks, sounds, the sun, time left before dark.
Plan: go back to the last known point, or stay put if it is late, foggy or you are hurt.
If you stay: make yourself visible and call 112.
w
Do not try shortcuts down steep unknown slopes: many accidents happen this way.

k: handrail catching feature navigation river ridge path handrails and catching features navigate with the landscape
b: ul
Handrail: a long feature you can follow, like a river, wall, ridge or forest edge.
Catching feature: something that stops you if you go too far, like a road or lake.
Aim off: aim slightly to one side of a target on a line; when you hit the line you know which way to turn.
Attack point: an easy-to-find feature near a hard-to-find target.

k: pacing distance steps count navigation fog measuring distance on foot count your steps
b: ul
Count every second step on 100 m of flat ground: that is your pace number (often 60-70).
Uphill, on snow or in heavy terrain you take more steps.
Use knots on a cord or beads to count each 100 m.
Time works too: on easy ground you walk about 4 km per hour.

k: coordinates gps latitude longitude position rescue utm giving your position coordinates rescuers understand
b: ul
Decimal format: 46.45320, 11.60512 (latitude first, then longitude).
Degrees-minutes-seconds: 46°27'11"N 11°36'18"E.
Read the numbers slowly, one by one, and say the format.
Also describe the place: valley, path number, landmarks, height.
Tent Mate shows your coordinates on the map and in SOS.

k: night dark headlamp walking navigation walking in the dark when the day runs out
b: ul
Always carry a headlamp and spare batteries.
Walk slower and stay on the path: navigation errors double at night.
Use red light to keep your night vision when you stop.
Stop if the terrain becomes difficult or you lose the path: wait for light.

s: Get low, get away from metal
k: lightning thunderstorm storm ridge summit metal cable thunderstorms in the mountains get low, get away from metal
b: ul
Afternoon storms are common in summer: start early, be off summits and ridges by early afternoon.
Count seconds between flash and thunder: under 30 seconds, you are in danger.
Leave summits, ridges and via ferrata cables; stay away from lone trees and metal.
Crouch on your insulating mat or pack, feet together, away from rock walls and water.
Groups: spread out at least 15 m apart.
Wait 30 minutes after the last thunder.

k: avalanche snow slope danger beacon shovel probe bulletin avalanche basics snow is not always safe
b: ul
Read the avalanche bulletin before any winter trip off marked pistes.
Most avalanches happen on slopes of 30-45°, often triggered by the victims.
Warning signs: recent avalanches, cracks spreading, 'whumpf' sounds, heavy new snow or wind, fast warming.
In avalanche terrain everyone needs a transceiver, shovel and probe, and training to use them.
Cross dangerous slopes one at a time.
w
If you are not trained in avalanche safety, stay on marked and secured routes in winter.

s: Old snow can be a slide
k: snowfield crossing slip crampons ice axe spring crossing snowfields old snow can be a slide
b: ul
In the morning old snow is often hard and icy; a slip can turn into a long slide onto rocks.
Kick steps firmly, lean into the slope less, keep your weight over your feet.
Without crampons and an ice axe, avoid steep snowfields with dangerous runouts.
Look below: where would you end up if you slipped?

s: Water is stronger than it looks
k: river stream crossing ford flood current crossing streams water is stronger than it looks
b: ul
Look for the widest, shallowest place, not the narrowest.
Unclip the hip belt so you can drop the pack.
Face upstream, use poles, move one point at a time.
Cross in the morning: snowmelt raises streams in the afternoon.
Water above the knee and fast is dangerous. If in doubt, do not cross.

k: rockfall scree falling rocks helmet gully rockfall and scree watch above, move fast below
b: ul
Wear a helmet in gullies, on via ferrata and below cliffs.
Move quickly and do not stop in rockfall zones.
If you knock a rock loose, shout 'ROCK!' (or 'SASSO!' in Italy) loudly.
Groups in gullies: stay close together or move one at a time so a rock cannot gather speed.
Rockfall increases with heat, thaw and after rain.

k: via ferrata cable lanyard harness helmet klettersteig via ferrata basics cables, clips and good habits
b: ul
You need a helmet, harness and a via ferrata set with energy absorber that meets the standard.
Always keep at least one carabiner clipped to the cable.
Only one person between two anchor points.
Check the weight limits of your set, especially for children and light people.
Do not start if thunderstorms are possible: the cable conducts lightning.

s: When the drop gets in your head
k: exposure vertigo fear heights exposed path exposure and vertigo when the drop gets in your head
b: ul
Look at your feet and the next holds, not into the void.
Breathe slowly and talk with your partner.
Three points of contact on exposed rock: two hands and a foot, or two feet and a hand.
If someone freezes, do not pull them: calm them, secure them, and get help if needed.
Turning back is a smart choice, not a failure.

k: glacier crevasse rope team ice glaciers hidden cracks under the snow
b: ul
Crevasses are often hidden under snow bridges, especially in the afternoon.
Never walk on a glacier unroped unless the ice is bare and dry.
Rope teams, crevasse rescue training and the right gear are needed.
Hire a mountain guide if you lack experience.

s: When you cannot see the trail
k: fog whiteout cloud visibility lost fog and whiteout when you cannot see the trail
b: ul
Note your position on the map before the fog arrives.
Follow the marked path closely: paint marks and cairns.
Use compass, GPS and your track back.
If you cannot see the next mark, stop and wait or go back along your track.
Stay together, close enough to see each other.

k: turnaround time decision summit fever plan the turnaround time decide before you leave
b: ul
Before you start, fix a time when you turn back, wherever you are.
Respect it even 50 m from the summit: most accidents happen on the way down, tired and late.
Plan enough time to be back before dark with a margin.
Tent Mate's arrival time and sunset warning help you decide.

k: solo alone hiking safety plan contact hiking alone freedom with a plan
b: ul
Leave your route and return time with someone, or use Tent Mate's automatic alarm.
Choose routes within your ability; nobody is there to help.
Carry a charged phone, power bank, headlamp and first aid kit.
Know where the phone has signal along the way.
Do not improvise new routes alone.

k: 112 call rescue emergency mountain rescue phone calling rescue what to say on 112
b: ol
Call 112: it works in all of Europe, even without your SIM in many countries.
Say who you are, what happened, how many people are hurt and their condition.
Say where you are: coordinates, path number, landmarks, height.
Say the weather and visibility where you are.
Keep the phone on and free; save battery; answer callbacks.
w
In Italy also install GeoResQ by the Soccorso Alpino. Text 112 if voice does not work; some countries support SMS to emergency numbers.

k: helicopter rescue landing signal yes no helicopter rescue help the crew help you
b: ul
Signal YES (need help): stand with both arms raised in a Y.
Signal NO (no help needed): one arm up, one arm down, making a slanted line.
Secure loose items: jackets, mats, tents fly away in the downwash.
Do not approach the helicopter until the crew signals you; always approach from the front, never from behind or uphill.

s: The sky tells you what is coming
k: clouds weather forecast cumulus cirrus storm reading the clouds the sky tells you what is coming
b: ul
Small white cumulus in the morning: fair weather.
Cumulus growing tall and dark by late morning: storms likely in the afternoon.
Anvil-shaped cumulonimbus: thunderstorm now or soon.
High thin cirrus spreading and thickening into a grey veil: a front is coming, often rain within 12-24 hours.
Lens-shaped clouds over peaks: strong winds at altitude.

k: storm signs thunder wind pressure temperature drop signs of a coming storm act before the first thunder
b: ul
Clouds building fast and darkening.
A sudden cold wind and drop in temperature.
Distant thunder: lightning can strike 15 km away.
Hair standing up or buzzing metal: lightning is imminent, move immediately.
Falling air pressure on your watch or phone.

k: foehn fohn wind warm dry alps foehn wind warm, dry and strong
b: ul
A warm, dry, often violent wind blowing down the lee side of the Alps.
It can melt snow fast and raise avalanche danger.
On the windward side of the range there is often heavy rain or snow at the same time.
Strong gusts on ridges: be careful on exposed passages.

k: wind chill cold temperature feels like frostbite wind chill wind makes cold colder
b: ul
At 0 °C with 40 km/h wind it feels like about -7 °C.
At -10 °C with 40 km/h wind it feels like about -21 °C: frostbite in under 30 minutes on bare skin.
A windproof layer is often worth more than an extra fleece.
Cover face, ears and hands in strong cold wind.

k: forecast mountain weather freezing level wind gusts mountain forecasts read more than the icon
b: ul
Look at the forecast for altitude, not the valley town.
Freezing level: above it rain becomes snow and paths can ice up.
Wind gusts over 60 km/h make ridges dangerous.
Thunderstorm risk: plan to be down early.
Check again the evening before and the morning you leave.
Tent Mate's mountain weather keeps the last forecast offline.

k: ten essentials gear checklist pack hiking the ten essentials what every pack should carry
b: ol
Navigation: map, compass, phone with offline maps.
Headlamp and spare batteries.
Sun protection: sunglasses, sunscreen, hat.
First aid kit.
Knife or multitool.
Fire: lighter and fire starter.
Emergency shelter: survival blanket or bivvy bag.
Extra food.
Extra water and a way to treat it.
Extra clothes: warm layer, rain jacket, hat and gloves.

k: backpack pack packing weight balance packing your backpack heavy close to the back
b: ul
Heavy items in the middle, close to your back.
Sleeping bag and light items at the bottom.
Rain jacket, first aid kit, snacks and map on top or in pockets.
Line the pack with a bin bag: covers leak.
Tighten the hip belt first: it should carry most of the weight.

k: boots shoes socks fit hiking feet boots and socks happy feet walk further
b: ul
Try boots in the afternoon, when feet are bigger, with your hiking socks.
Your toes must not touch the front on a downhill slope.
Break new boots in before a long trip.
Wool or synthetic socks, never cotton.
Lace the boot tighter for downhill to stop your foot sliding.

k: first aid kit contents bandage plasters first aid kit small, complete, checked
b: ul
Plasters, blister plasters and tape.
Sterile dressings, an elastic bandage and a triangular bandage.
Disinfectant wipes, tweezers or tick hook, small scissors.
Gloves and a survival blanket.
Painkillers, antihistamine, personal medicines.
Check expiry dates every season.

k: headlamp torch battery power bank phone headlamp and batteries light is safety
b: ul
Carry a headlamp even on short day hikes.
Lithium batteries work better in the cold.
Keep the phone warm and in airplane mode to save battery when you do not need signal.
A small power bank doubles your phone's life.

k: food energy calories snacks hiking eat eating on the trail small and often
b: ul
A day of hiking burns 2,500-4,000 kcal.
Eat a small snack every hour rather than one big meal.
Mix quick sugars with fats and protein: nuts, cheese, dried fruit, bars.
In the cold your body needs more energy: eat before you feel weak.

s: Only what you know for sure
k: foraging wild food edible plants berries rules foraging safely only what you know for sure
b: ul
Eat a wild plant only if you are 100% sure what it is.
Learn the deadly look-alikes first.
Pick away from roads, sprayed fields and dog walks.
Take only a small part; many plants are protected.
Wash everything well; in some areas the fox tapeworm is a risk with low-growing berries.
w
Tent Mate's scan helps you learn, but never decide from a photo alone whether something is safe to eat.

k: mushroom fungi picking rules poisonous amanita mushroom rules doubt means no
b: ul
Deadly mushrooms like the death cap can look harmless and taste good.
Never eat a wild mushroom without an expert check: in Italy, ASL mycological offices check them for free.
Rules on picking differ by region: permits, limits per day and protected areas.
Use a basket, not a plastic bag, so spores spread and mushrooms do not rot.

k: food storage bear canister animals mice camp storing food from animals keep wildlife wild
b: ul
Never keep food in the tent where bears live.
Use a bear canister or hang food 4 m high and 2 m from the trunk where required.
Cook and eat at least 60 m from where you sleep in bear country.
Mice, foxes and birds love open food in huts and camps too.

s: A loop that does not slip
k: bowline knot loop rope rescue bowline a loop that does not slip
b: ol
Make a small loop in the rope (the rabbit hole), with the working end on top.
Pass the end up through the loop (the rabbit comes out of the hole).
Take it around behind the standing part (around the tree).
Bring it back down through the small loop (back into the hole).
Pull tight and leave a long tail.

k: clove hitch knot pole tarp clove hitch quick tie to a pole
b: ul
Wrap the rope around the pole, cross over itself, wrap again and tuck under the second wrap.
Fast to tie and adjust; good for starting lashings and tarp lines.
It can slip under changing loads: add a half hitch for safety.

k: taut line hitch knot guy line tent adjust taut-line hitch adjustable tent lines
b: ul
Pass the rope around the peg, then wrap the end twice around the standing line inside the loop.
Finish with one more wrap outside the loop.
Slide the knot to tighten or loosen the guy line; it holds under load.

k: figure eight knot stopper loop climbing figure-eight knot the climber's knot
b: ul
Stopper: a figure eight at the end of a rope stops it slipping through a device.
Figure-eight loop: strong, easy to check, used to tie into a harness.
Always leave a tail of at least 10 cm.

k: truckers hitch knot ridge line tension trucker's hitch pull a line very tight
b: ul
Make a loop in the standing part of the line.
Pass the end around the anchor and back through the loop: this gives a 2:1 pulley.
Pull tight and lock it with two half hitches.
Perfect for tarp ridge lines and tying loads.

s: Join two ends of the same rope
k: reef knot square knot bandage join reef (square) knot join two ends of the same rope
b: ul
Right over left and under, then left over right and under.
Good for bandages and tying bundles.
Not safe for joining two ropes under load: use a double fisherman's knot instead.

k: bear brown bear encounter trentino abruzzo bears avoid surprises
b: ul
Make noise on paths with poor visibility so you do not surprise a bear.
If you see one far away: do not approach, leave calmly the way you came.
If close: do not run, speak calmly, move away slowly sideways, keep the group together.
Never get between a mother and cubs.
If attacked by a brown bear that is defending itself: lie face down, protect your neck with your hands, keep the pack on.
Report sightings to the local forest service.

k: wolf wolves encounter wolves shy, rarely seen
b: ul
Wolves usually avoid people.
If you meet one: stay still, make yourself big, speak loudly, then move away without running.
Keep dogs on a lead in wolf areas.
Never feed wildlife: it is how animals lose their fear of people.

k: viper adder snake bite venom vipers and snake bites rare but serious
b: ul
Vipers bite only when stepped on or handled. Watch where you put hands and feet on sunny rocks.
After a bite: keep calm, keep the person still, remove rings and watches.
Immobilize the limb like a fracture, keep it at heart level.
Do not cut, suck, apply ice or a tourniquet.
Call 112: anti-venom is given in hospital if needed.

k: cows cattle guard dog patou sheep pasture cows and guard dogs respect the herd
b: ul
Do not walk between cows and calves; keep at least 20 m.
Keep your dog on a lead, but let it go if cows charge.
Livestock guard dogs protect flocks: stop, stay calm, do not stare or wave sticks, and walk around the flock slowly.
Close gates behind you.

k: wasp hornet nest sting wasps and hornets leave the nest alone
b: ul
Do not swat: move away calmly.
Ground nests are common on paths in late summer: watch for a stream of insects from a hole.
If attacked by many: run away and protect your face. Do not jump into water.
Many stings or any allergic sign: call 112.

k: ticks prevention repellent clothing check preventing tick bites check every evening
b: ul
Long light-coloured trousers tucked into socks.
Repellent on skin and permethrin on clothes where allowed.
Stay in the middle of paths, away from tall grass and bushes.
Check your whole body in the evening, including hair, armpits and behind the knees.

k: leave no trace principles environment leave no trace seven principles
b: ol
Plan ahead and prepare.
Travel and camp on durable surfaces.
Dispose of waste properly: pack it in, pack it out.
Leave what you find.
Minimize campfire impacts.
Respect wildlife.
Be considerate of other visitors.

k: toilet poop cathole outdoors hygiene toilet in nature dig, cover, pack it out
b: ul
Go at least 60 m from water, paths and camps.
Dig a hole 15-20 cm deep, then cover it.
Pack out toilet paper and wipes in a sealed bag.
On glaciers and in high rocky areas, carry everything out.
Wash or gel your hands after.

k: children kids family hiking hiking with children their pace, their adventure
b: ul
Plan short routes with goals: a lake, a hut, animals.
Count about 1 km per year of age as a rough daily limit for young children.
More breaks, more snacks, more layers than for adults.
Children cool down and get sunburnt faster.
Give them a whistle and teach them to stay put and blow it if lost.

k: dog hiking pets paws water lead hiking with a dog good boy, good plan
b: ul
Check the rules: dogs may be banned in parks or need a lead.
Carry water for the dog; streams are not always available.
Rocks, snow and hot ground hurt paws: check them on breaks.
Keep it on a lead near livestock and wildlife.
Watch for heat: dogs overheat faster than people.

k: group hiking leader slowest pace walking in a group nobody left behind
b: ul
The slowest person sets the pace and walks near the front.
Agree on meeting points at every junction.
Someone experienced walks last.
Count heads at every stop.
Decide together, but name one person to make final safety calls.
